title: Best Hangover Patch? Bytox, PatchAid and Others Compared
excerpt: Bytox, PatchAid, marketplace multipacks and DHM patches compared on what is checkable: labels, claims, cost per night, adhesion, and the evidence (there is none).
metaDescription: Bytox, PatchAid and other hangover patches compared on labels, cost, adhesion and evidence. Why no patch can honestly be called the best, and what to try.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no "best" hangover patch in the sense of one that has been shown to work. Not one brand, Bytox included, has published a placebo-controlled trial showing its patch reduces hangovers, and none has published blood tests showing how much of its vitamins actually get through your skin. So when we compare brands, we can't rank them on effectiveness. What we *can* compare is everything else that's checkable: how open each brand is about what's in the patch, how much you pay per night, how well the adhesive holds, how bold the marketing claims are, and how easy it is to get your money back.

**The quick verdict:** if you're set on trying a patch, Bytox is the most established name and the most consistent buying experience, PatchAid is the pick if you already like vitamin patches and want a company that sells them as its core business, and cheap marketplace multipacks are the riskiest buy because labels and sellers change constantly. If what you really want is a better morning, a plain oral B-complex costs a fraction of the price, and an oral supplement such as DHM is a more reasonable thing to try because it doesn't depend on getting through your skin.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article compares consumer products and summarizes general research. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Talk to a doctor before using any supplement product if you are pregnant, have a skin condition, have liver or kidney disease, or take prescription medicine. No patch lowers your blood alcohol level or makes it safe to drive. Seek urgent care for signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, or someone you can't wake up. In an emergency, call 911.

## How We Compared Hangover Patches

We did not run a lab test or a clinical trial, and you should be wary of any "we tested 20 patches" article that claims to have measured which one works best. Nobody can tell that from a few nights out, because hangovers vary so much from one night to the next. For the full science on whether patches can work at all, see our companion piece, [Do Hangover Patches Work?](/never-hungover/do-hangover-patches-work). This page assumes you've read the caveats and still want to know how the brands differ.

Here are the criteria we used, in order of how much they matter:

1. **Ingredient transparency.** Does the brand list every ingredient with an amount per patch, or does it hide behind a "proprietary blend"? A blend tells you what's in the adhesive but not how much.
2. **Evidence and claims.** Does the brand publish any absorption data or trial results? (None we know of do.) Does the marketing stay within reason, or does it promise to "block" hangovers or claim the skin absorbs vitamins many times better than the gut?
3. **Cost per night.** Patches are sold in packs of different sizes, so the sticker price is misleading. What matters is the cost of one night's use, compared with the alternatives.
4. **Adhesion and skin comfort.** A patch that falls off on the dance floor is worthless even on its own terms. Peeling and skin redness are the most common complaints in user reviews across every brand.
5. **Buying experience.** Is the brand easy to buy directly, with a clear return policy, or is it a rotating cast of marketplace sellers?

Formulas and prices change, sometimes several times a year. Treat every brand description below as a starting point and **read the current label before you buy**.

## Hangover Patch Brands Compared at a Glance

| Brand type | What it usually contains | Transparency | Published evidence | Typical value | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bytox** | B-vitamin complex plus extras such as plant extracts (check current label) | Lists ingredients; the best-known brand | No published trials or absorption data | Mid to high per night | People who want the most established name |
| **PatchAid (hangover-style patch)** | B vitamins and related nutrients from a company that mainly sells vitamin patches | Lists ingredients and amounts | No published hangover trials | Mid per night, better in bulk | People who already use vitamin patches |
| **Marketplace multipacks** (generic and private-label) | Varies widely; often a B-complex with plant extracts | Often weak; amounts may be missing | None | Lowest sticker price | Bargain hunters willing to gamble |
| **Patches that list DHM** | DHM plus B vitamins or extracts | Mixed | No evidence DHM crosses skin | Mid to high | Not recommended; take DHM by mouth instead |
| **Oral B-complex tablet** (for comparison) | Full B-complex in known amounts | High | Absorption is well established | A few cents a day | Anyone who wants B vitamins |
| **Oral DHM supplement** (for comparison) | DHM, sometimes with L-cysteine or electrolytes | Usually high | Limited human data, promising animal research | About $1 to $2 a serving | People who want a hangover-specific supplement |

The rows for oral products are there on purpose. Comparing patches only with other patches hides the most important fact: every patch is competing with a cheaper pill that delivers its ingredients reliably.

## Bytox Review: The Category Leader

Bytox is the name most people mean when they say "hangover patch." It's a US brand sold on its own website and through large retailers, and it's built around a B-vitamin complex with a few supporting ingredients. Because it's the best-known product, most of the online debate about whether hangover patches work is really a debate about Bytox. For a full single-brand look, see our [Bytox review](/never-hungover/bytox-review).

**Pros:**

- **Most established brand.** It has been around longer than most competitors, has consistent packaging, and is easy to buy from reputable sellers, which lowers the risk of counterfeits or relabeled stock.
- **Ingredients are listed.** You can see what you're putting on your skin and check it for allergens.
- **Convenient.** One patch before you go out, no pills to remember the next morning.
- **Plenty of reviews.** With a large number of user reports, you can at least get a realistic sense of adhesion and skin tolerance.

**Cons:**

- **No clinical evidence.** We're not aware of any published, placebo-controlled trial of Bytox, or any published data showing how much of its vitamins reach your blood.
- **Costs much more than pills.** One night's patch typically costs many times more than a day's dose of an oral B-complex.
- **Mixed reviews.** Some users swear by it. Many others notice no difference, especially after heavier nights, and peeling during sweaty nights out is a recurring complaint.
- **The core ingredient problem.** B vitamins are water-soluble, and the outer layer of skin is built to keep water-soluble molecules out. Vitamin B12 in particular is a large molecule that is unlikely to cross intact skin in a useful amount.

**Our take:** if you're going to buy a hangover patch, Bytox is the least risky purchase in the category. But "least risky patch" is not the same as "works." We wouldn't spend money on it expecting a noticeably better morning.

## PatchAid: The Vitamin-Patch Specialist

PatchAid is a company whose whole business is vitamin patches. Its range includes multivitamin, B12, and other single-purpose patches, and it sells a hangover-oriented option alongside them. That focus is both its strength and its limitation.

**Pros:**

- **Clear labeling.** Specialist patch companies tend to list each ingredient with an amount per patch, which makes it easier to compare with what you'd get from a pill.
- **Bulk pricing.** Larger packs bring the cost per night down, which matters if you'd use them often.
- **A familiar brand for regular patch users.** If you already use a PatchAid multivitamin patch for daily nutrition, adding their hangover-style patch is simple.

**Cons:**

- **Same absorption question as every other brand.** Being a patch specialist doesn't change how skin works. We're not aware of published blood-level data showing that a hangover-style vitamin patch delivers a meaningful dose.
- **Patches for daily nutrition have a poor track record.** A 2019 study in *Obesity Surgery* compared multivitamin patches with oral multivitamins in people after weight-loss surgery, a group with every reason to benefit from a non-oral route. After a year, the patch group was more likely to be deficient in several nutrients than the pill group. That study wasn't about hangovers, but it is the best real-world test of vitamin patches we have, and patches lost.
- **Not hangover-specific science.** The formula is still built around B vitamins, which haven't been shown to prevent hangovers even when swallowed.

**Our take:** a reasonable choice for people who already like vitamin patches and value clear labels. Not a reason to start using patches if you don't already.

## Marketplace Multipacks: Cheap, Variable, and Hard to Trust

Search "hangover patch" on Amazon or any large marketplace and you'll find dozens of listings with names like "party patch," "recovery patch," or "after party patch," often in 30-count or bigger packs at low prices. Many come from private-label sellers who buy generic patches and add their own branding.

**Pros:**

- **Lowest sticker price.** Cost per patch is often well below the established brands.
- **Easy to find and fast to ship.**

**Cons:**

- **Ingredient lists can be vague.** Some listings name ingredients without giving amounts. Some describe a "proprietary blend." That tells you nothing about the dose.
- **Listings change.** Sellers can change the product, the formula, or the supplier while keeping the same listing and its old reviews. The glowing review you're reading may be about a different patch.
- **Bolder claims.** Some listings promise to "block" hangovers, "neutralize" alcohol, or absorb "10 times better" than pills. No published evidence supports claims like these for any patch, and bolder marketing is a warning sign, not a feature.
- **More adhesive and skin complaints.** Cheaper adhesives are a common source of peeling and redness in reviews.

**Our take:** the riskiest way to try a patch. If you do, buy from a listing with a full ingredient list with amounts, a clear seller name, and a return policy, and ignore listings that make medical-sounding promises.

## Patches That List DHM

A few newer patches add dihydromyricetin (DHM), the plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that this site focuses on. It's an understandable marketing move, since DHM has a much stronger hangover-specific research base than B vitamins. But putting it in a patch doesn't make sense with what's known.

- **We're not aware of any published evidence that DHM gets through skin in useful amounts.** DHM is fairly water-loving, which is the wrong profile for skin delivery.
- **It's poorly absorbed even by mouth.** That's why oral DHM products use doses in the hundreds of milligrams to 1,000 mg. A small adhesive patch can't hold anything close to that.
- **The DHM research is oral.** The animal studies that made DHM interesting, including the widely cited 2012 rat study in the *Journal of Neuroscience*, gave it by mouth or by injection, not through the skin.

**Our take:** skip DHM patches. If DHM interests you, take it by mouth, where at least the dose is known. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts.

## Best Hangover Patch on Amazon: How to Shop Smart

Most people searching for the best hangover patch end up on Amazon. Star ratings there mostly measure how well a product is marketed and how often placebo kicks in, not whether it works. Here's how to use the listings well:

- **Read the one- and two-star reviews first.** They tell you about adhesion, skin reactions, and whether the product changed recently. Five-star reviews mostly tell you someone had a good morning, which happens with or without a patch.
- **Look for amounts, not just ingredients.** If the listing doesn't say how many milligrams or micrograms of each vitamin are in one patch, move on.
- **Work out the cost per night.** Divide the price by the number of patches. Then compare it with an oral B-complex, which usually costs a few cents per tablet.
- **Check the seller.** Buying from the brand's own storefront or a well-known retailer lowers the risk of counterfeit or expired stock.
- **Be skeptical of absorption claims.** "Bypasses the stomach" and "absorbs better than pills" are the two most common claims in the category. We're not aware of any hangover patch brand that has published evidence for either one.

## Hangover Patch vs Pills vs Drink Mixes

Patches are only one of several "night out" products. Here's how they compare with the other common options on the things that matter.

| | Hangover patch | Oral B-complex | Oral DHM supplement | Electrolyte drink mix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| What it targets | Vitamins alcohol may deplete | Same vitamins | How the body handles alcohol | Fluids and salts |
| Does the dose reach you? | Unknown; no published data | Yes, reliably | Yes, though absorption is modest | Yes |
| Hangover-specific evidence | None | Weak | Limited human data, promising animal research | Helps rehydration, not a hangover cure |
| Typical cost per night | Often $1 to $3 | A few cents | About $1 to $2 | About $1 to $2 |
| Main downsides | Peeling, skin irritation, unknown absorption | Can upset an empty stomach | Mixed evidence; check with a doctor if on medication | Sugar in some brands |

The pattern is consistent. Patches cost about as much as the hangover-specific products but carry less evidence than even a basic vitamin pill. If you want help with fluids, our [Liquid IV for hangover review](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover) covers what electrolyte mixes can and can't do. If you prefer pills, our [best hangover pills guide](/never-hungover/best-hangover-pills) compares the oral options.

## Does Bytox Work Better Than Cheaper Patches?

There's no evidence either way, because neither Bytox nor its cheaper rivals have been tested in a published trial. The ingredients in most hangover patches overlap heavily: a B-complex, often vitamin C, sometimes plant extracts. If the active ingredients are similar and none of them has been shown to get through skin in useful amounts, the price difference is mostly paying for brand trust, consistency, and customer service.

That brand trust isn't worthless. A consistent product from a known company means you get what the label says is in the adhesive, and you can get a refund if it irritates your skin. But it doesn't buy you a better-proven effect.

## How to Use a Hangover Patch (If You Try One)

If you've weighed the evidence and still want to try one, use it in a way that gives you the fairest test and the fewest side effects:

1. **Apply it to clean, dry, hair-free skin** a little while before you start drinking. The inner wrist, upper arm, and the side of the torso are common spots. Avoid broken or irritated skin.
2. **Press it down for several seconds** so the adhesive bonds fully. Lotion, sweat, and body oil are the main reasons patches peel.
3. **Follow the label on how long to wear it.** Remove it if you notice redness, itching, or burning.
4. **Keep doing the things that actually help:** eat a real meal, alternate drinks with water, and pace yourself. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.
5. **Don't drink more because you're wearing it.** This is the biggest real risk with any hangover product.

### A fairer way to judge whether it helps you

If you want to know whether a patch does anything for you, compare similar nights: same amount and type of drink, similar food, similar bedtime, with and without the patch. Write down how you felt the next morning. A handful of comparisons like that won't be a clinical trial, but it's far better than judging from one good morning.

## Who Should Skip Hangover Patches

Patches are low risk for most healthy adults, mostly because so little is probably absorbed. But some people should skip them or check with a doctor first:

- **People with sensitive skin or eczema**, since adhesive reactions are the most common side effect.
- **People who are pregnant or breastfeeding**, as with any supplement product.
- **People getting blood work done soon**, if the patch contains biotin, because high-dose biotin can interfere with some lab tests. Mention it to your doctor.
- **People already taking several B-vitamin products**, such as a multivitamin, a B-complex, and B-vitamin energy drinks. It's worth adding up long-term vitamin B6 intake, since very high oral doses over long periods can cause nerve problems.
- **People who drink heavily on a regular basis.** If you're worried about thiamine or folate, a patch is the wrong tool. Talk to a doctor, who can recommend a reliable supplement or test your levels.

## Better Options Than Any Hangover Patch

No product cures a hangover, and the only sure way to avoid one is to drink less. But if you're comparing patches because you want a better morning, these steps have more behind them than any patch brand:

- **Pace yourself and eat first.** How much you drink and how fast are the biggest factors in how bad a hangover gets.
- **Hydrate.** Water between drinks and before bed won't cure a hangover, but dehydration makes the headache and fatigue worse.
- **Choose lighter drinks.** Clear spirits generally contain fewer congeners, the extra compounds found in darker drinks like whiskey and red wine.
- **Protect your sleep.** Alcohol disrupts the second half of the night, so stopping earlier helps.
- **Consider an oral supplement with at least some human data.** Our [hangover supplements guide](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025) walks through the popular options and how strong, or weak, the evidence is for each.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM is the reason this site exists, so here's a straight account. Most of the research behind it comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It is not a proven hangover cure. We think it's a more reasonable thing to try than a vitamin patch for two simple reasons: it's taken by mouth, which avoids the skin problem entirely, and it's aimed at how the body handles alcohol rather than at topping up vitamins most well-fed people aren't short of. For a balanced look at the research, see our [honest review of whether DHM works](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025).

If you'd like to try it, timing and dose matter more than the brand. Two popular choices are [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which pairs DHM with L-cysteine, and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM timing guide](/never-hungover/when-to-take-dhm-timing-guide-2025) explains when to take it relative to drinking. Check with your doctor first if you take prescription medicine or have liver disease, and don't treat any supplement as permission to drink more.

## The Bottom Line

- **No hangover patch has published evidence that it works,** so no brand can honestly be called the best at preventing hangovers.
- **Bytox is the most established and lowest-risk purchase** in the category if you want to try one.
- **PatchAid suits people who already use vitamin patches** and want clear labels and bulk pricing.
- **Generic marketplace patches are the biggest gamble,** with vague labels, shifting listings, and the boldest claims.
- **Skip patches that list DHM.** There's no evidence DHM crosses skin, and the dose a patch can hold is tiny.
- **A cheap oral B-complex beats every patch** if you want B vitamins, and an oral supplement like DHM is a more reasonable hangover-specific option.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best hangover patch?**

There's no brand with published evidence that it reduces hangovers, so none can honestly be called the best at that. If you want to try one, Bytox is the most established and consistent option, and PatchAid suits people who already use vitamin patches. Generic marketplace patches are the riskiest buy because labels and sellers change often. An oral B-complex delivers the same vitamins far more reliably and cheaply.

**Is Bytox worth it?**

Bytox is the best-known hangover patch and a safer purchase than anonymous marketplace patches, but there's no published clinical trial showing it works, and no published data on how much of its vitamins reach your blood. User reviews are mixed, with peeling a common complaint. If your goal is a better morning, the money is better spent on food, water, and an oral supplement with at least some human data.

**What is the best hangover patch on Amazon?**

Star ratings on Amazon mostly reflect marketing and placebo rather than effectiveness. If you shop there, choose a listing that gives the amount of each ingredient per patch, comes from the brand's own storefront or a well-known seller, has a clear return policy, and avoids claims like "blocks hangovers." Read the low-star reviews for adhesion and skin problems before buying.

**Are hangover patches better than pills?**

No. Oral vitamins are absorbed reliably, cost a few cents a day, and you know roughly what dose you're getting. Patches cost much more per night and no brand has published proof of how much reaches your blood. In the best real-world test we know of, a 2019 study in Obesity Surgery, people using vitamin patches were more likely to end up deficient than people taking pills.

**Do DHM hangover patches work?**

There's no good evidence that they do. We're not aware of any published data showing DHM gets through skin in useful amounts, and oral DHM products use doses of several hundred milligrams to 1,000 mg because it's poorly absorbed even when swallowed. A patch can't hold anywhere near that. If you want to try DHM, take it by mouth.

**Are hangover patches safe?**

For most healthy adults they're unlikely to cause harm, mainly because so little is probably absorbed. The common problems are skin redness or itching from the adhesive. The bigger risk is feeling protected and drinking more. If you're pregnant, have a skin condition, take prescription medicine, or have blood work coming up while using a biotin-containing patch, check with your doctor first.

**Does Bytox work better than cheaper hangover patches?**

There's no evidence either way, because neither Bytox nor its cheaper competitors have published trial results. Most hangover patches share a similar B-vitamin base. Paying more for Bytox mainly buys you a consistent product, clearer labeling, and a reliable seller, not a better-proven effect.

**When should you put on a hangover patch?**

Brands generally suggest applying it to clean, dry, hair-free skin a little before you start drinking and wearing it for the time on the label. Press it down firmly, avoid broken or irritated skin, and remove it if your skin reacts. Keep eating, drinking water, and pacing yourself, because those habits matter far more than any patch.
